rice.season: Kharif: sow the nursery in June and transplant 25 to 30 day old seedlings in July. A rabi or summer crop is also possible where irrigation is assured.
rice.soil: Clay or clay loam that holds water, pH 5.5 to 7. Level the field well so water stays even.
rice.water: Keep about 5 cm of standing water from transplanting to flowering. Drain the field about 10 days before harvest.
rice.fertilizer: Give nitrogen in three splits: at transplanting, at tillering and at panicle start. Apply phosphorus and potash once as a basal dose.
rice.pests: Watch for stem borer, brown planthopper and blast disease. Use healthy seed, balanced nitrogen and clean bunds.
rice.harvest: Ready 110 to 150 days after sowing when about 80% of the grains turn straw yellow. Harvest before grains start to shatter.
rice.tip: Transplant young seedlings in straight rows, 1 or 2 per hill, for better tillering and easier weeding.

maize.season: Kharif (June to July) in most areas. Rabi (October to November) and spring sowing also work where irrigation is available.
maize.soil: Fertile, well-drained loam, pH 5.8 to 7. Even a day or two of waterlogging harms young plants.
maize.water: Needs regular moisture, especially at knee-high stage, tasseling and grain filling. Never let the field flood.
maize.fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in two or three splits (sowing, knee-high, tasseling) and phosphorus and potash at sowing. Add farmyard manure before sowing.
maize.pests: Fall armyworm, stem borer and leaf blights are common. Check the leaf whorls every week and destroy egg masses early.
maize.harvest: Harvest 90 to 120 days after sowing when husks dry and kernels are hard. Dry cobs well before storage.
maize.tip: Sow in rows about 60 x 20 cm apart and earth up around plants at knee-high stage to stop them falling over.

chickpea.season: Rabi: sow from mid-October to mid-November after the monsoon, using the moisture stored in the soil.
chickpea.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy loam, pH 6 to 8. Avoid waterlogged or salty fields.
chickpea.water: Usually grown on stored soil moisture. One or two light irrigations at branching and pod filling help; too much water lowers yield.
chickpea.fertilizer: Needs little nitrogen because it makes its own. Apply phosphorus at sowing and treat the seed with Rhizobium culture.
chickpea.pests: Pod borer and wilt are the main problems. Use wilt-resistant varieties, treat the seed and set up bird perches.
chickpea.harvest: Harvest 100 to 140 days after sowing when leaves turn yellow-brown and pods rattle when shaken.
chickpea.tip: Pinch off the tips of the main shoots 30 to 40 days after sowing to get more branches and pods.

kidneybeans.season: A cool-season crop: sow in October to November in the plains, and from March to June in the hills.
kidneybeans.soil: Well-drained loam rich in organic matter, pH 5.5 to 6.5. It does not tolerate waterlogging or salty soil.
kidneybeans.water: Irrigate lightly at flowering and pod formation. Avoid wet soil at sowing because seeds can rot.
kidneybeans.fertilizer: Apply phosphorus and a small dose of nitrogen at sowing and treat the seed with Rhizobium. Too much nitrogen gives leaves but few pods.
kidneybeans.pests: Watch for aphids, pod borer, rust and anthracnose. Use clean seed and rotate with cereals.
kidneybeans.harvest: Harvest 90 to 120 days after sowing when pods turn yellow and dry. Thresh only when plants are fully dry.
kidneybeans.tip: Sow in rows 30 to 45 cm apart so air moves between plants and disease stays low.

pigeonpeas.season: Kharif: sow in June to July with the first monsoon rains.
pigeonpeas.soil: Well-drained loam or black soil, pH 6.5 to 7.5. Waterlogging can kill the crop.
pigeonpeas.water: Mostly rain-fed. Irrigate at flowering and pod filling if there is a long dry spell.
pigeonpeas.fertilizer: Needs only a small starter dose of nitrogen with phosphorus at sowing. Use Rhizobium-treated seed.
pigeonpeas.pests: Pod borer, pod fly and wilt are common. Use resistant varieties and do not grow it on the same field every year.
pigeonpeas.harvest: Harvest 150 to 280 days after sowing, depending on the variety, when about 75 to 80% of pods turn brown.
pigeonpeas.tip: Intercrop with a short-duration crop such as green gram or sorghum to earn income while pigeon pea grows slowly.

mothbeans.season: Kharif: sow in July with the first monsoon rains. It suits dry regions such as Rajasthan.
mothbeans.soil: Light sandy or sandy loam soil, pH 6 to 8. It grows in poor, dry soils but not in waterlogged ones.
mothbeans.water: Very drought hardy and usually rain-fed. Give one irrigation at flowering only if a long dry spell occurs.
mothbeans.fertilizer: A small dose of phosphorus at sowing is enough. Seed treatment with Rhizobium helps; extra nitrogen is rarely needed.
mothbeans.pests: Yellow mosaic virus, leaf spots and aphids occur. Use resistant varieties and control whitefly.
mothbeans.harvest: Harvest 60 to 90 days after sowing when most pods turn brown.
mothbeans.tip: Sow in rows 30 to 45 cm apart and weed once at about 20 days. It uses very little water and fits dry farms.

mungbean.season: Kharif (June to July), or summer (March to April) where irrigated. It matures in about 60 to 70 days.
mungbean.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy loam, pH 6.2 to 7.2. Avoid waterlogged and salty soil.
mungbean.water: Needs little water: one or two irrigations in summer, at flowering and pod filling. Stop irrigating once pods mature.
mungbean.fertilizer: Apply phosphorus at sowing and treat the seed with Rhizobium. It makes its own nitrogen, so avoid extra urea.
mungbean.pests: Yellow mosaic virus spread by whitefly is the main risk, along with aphids and leaf spot. Choose resistant varieties and remove infected plants.
mungbean.harvest: Pick pods when they turn black or brown, in two or three pickings, 60 to 70 days after sowing.
mungbean.tip: Grow it as a short rotation crop between cereals. It adds nitrogen to the soil for the next crop.

blackgram.season: Kharif (June to July), or summer (February to March) where irrigated.
blackgram.soil: Well-drained clay loam or loam, pH 6.5 to 7.8. Avoid waterlogged fields.
blackgram.water: Mostly rain-fed. Irrigate at flowering and pod filling if rain fails, and drain extra water quickly.
blackgram.fertilizer: Apply phosphorus at sowing and treat the seed with Rhizobium. Skip heavy nitrogen.
blackgram.pests: Yellow mosaic virus, powdery mildew and leaf spots are common. Use resistant varieties and control whitefly early.
blackgram.harvest: Harvest 70 to 90 days after sowing when most pods turn black and dry.
blackgram.tip: Keep the field weed-free for the first 30 days, since young plants grow slowly.

lentil.season: Rabi: sow in late October to November and harvest in March to April.
lentil.soil: Well-drained loam to clay loam, pH 6 to 8. It dislikes waterlogging and strongly acidic soil.
lentil.water: Grown mostly on stored moisture. One or two light irrigations at branching and pod filling raise yield.
lentil.fertilizer: Apply phosphorus at sowing and treat the seed with Rhizobium. Very little nitrogen is needed.
lentil.pests: Watch for aphids, pod borer, rust and wilt. Use treated seed and resistant varieties, and rotate crops.
lentil.harvest: Harvest 100 to 130 days after sowing when leaves and pods turn yellow-brown. Cut early in the day to reduce shattering.
lentil.tip: Sow right after the paddy harvest on the leftover moisture to save time and irrigation.

pomegranate.season: Plant saplings in July to August or February to March. Choose the flowering season (bahar) by water availability.
pomegranate.soil: Well-drained sandy loam or loam, pH 6.5 to 7.5. It tolerates some salt but not waterlogging.
pomegranate.water: Drip irrigation works best. Keep moisture steady during fruit growth, because sudden swings split the fruits.
pomegranate.fertilizer: Give farmyard manure at planting and every year, with nitrogen, phosphorus and potash split across the year. Add zinc and boron if leaves show deficiency.
pomegranate.pests: Bacterial blight, fruit borer and thrips are common. Remove infected fruits, prune for airflow and avoid overhead watering.
pomegranate.harvest: Fruits are ready 5 to 6 months after flowering when the skin turns slightly yellow-red and gives a metallic sound when tapped.
pomegranate.tip: Prune lightly after harvest and keep the orchard clean to reduce bacterial blight.

banana.season: Plant suckers or tissue-culture plants from June to August, or in February to March. Avoid peak winter and peak heat.
banana.soil: Deep, well-drained, fertile loam rich in organic matter, pH 6 to 7.5. Waterlogged or very sandy soil gives poor bunches.
banana.water: Needs regular water: about every 3 to 5 days in summer and weekly in cool weather. Drip irrigation saves water.
banana.fertilizer: A heavy feeder of potassium and nitrogen. Apply in small splits from the second month until flowering, with plenty of compost.
banana.pests: Panama wilt, sigatoka leaf spot, rhizome weevil and nematodes are common. Plant disease-free tissue-culture plants and remove diseased leaves.
banana.harvest: The bunch is ready 11 to 14 months after planting when the fingers turn round and lose their angles.
banana.tip: Keep only one follower sucker per plant, remove the extra ones, and prop the plant so heavy bunches do not fall in the wind.

mango.season: Plant grafted saplings in July to September with the monsoon. Trees flower in winter and fruit ripens from April to July.
mango.soil: Deep, well-drained loam or alluvial soil, pH 5.5 to 7.5. Avoid waterlogged and shallow rocky soil.
mango.water: Water young trees weekly in dry months. Mature trees need little water just before and during flowering; irrigate again after fruit set.
mango.fertilizer: Apply farmyard manure and NPK around the edge of the canopy every year after harvest. Add zinc or boron if needed.
mango.pests: Mango hopper, powdery mildew, anthracnose and fruit fly are common. Keep the orchard clean and spray at flowering as local experts advise.
mango.harvest: Fruits mature 100 to 150 days after fruit set. Pick when the shoulders are full and a few fruits ripen naturally, leaving a short stalk.
mango.tip: Prune dead branches and thin dense growth after harvest so sunlight and air reduce disease and improve fruit size.

grapes.season: Plant rooted cuttings in the cool months. In peninsular India vines are pruned twice: for growth in April and for fruit in October, with harvest from February to April.
grapes.soil: Well-drained sandy loam or gravelly soil, pH 6.5 to 7.5. Poor drainage and high salts harm the roots.
grapes.water: Use drip irrigation. Give regular water during shoot and berry growth and reduce it near ripening to improve sweetness.
grapes.fertilizer: Apply farmyard manure after pruning and balanced NPK in stages, with extra potash while berries develop.
grapes.pests: Downy and powdery mildew, thrips and mealybugs are common. Train vines for good airflow and spray preventively as local experts advise.
grapes.harvest: Pick bunches when berries are fully coloured and taste sweet and the stalk starts to brown. Cut in the cool morning.
grapes.tip: Thin bunches and remove extra shoots so the remaining berries grow bigger and leaves dry faster.

watermelon.season: Sow in January to March for a summer crop, or October to December in warm regions.
watermelon.soil: Well-drained sandy loam rich in organic matter, pH 6 to 7. Heavy clay and waterlogging cause rot.
watermelon.water: Water regularly during vine growth and flowering, then reduce water as fruits ripen to keep them sweet.
watermelon.fertilizer: Apply farmyard manure and phosphorus at sowing, then split nitrogen and potash during vine growth and fruit set.
watermelon.pests: Fruit fly, red pumpkin beetle, powdery mildew and fusarium wilt are common. Use mulch and resistant varieties, and do not repeat melons on the same field.
watermelon.harvest: Ready 75 to 100 days after sowing when the tendril near the fruit dries, the underside turns creamy yellow and tapping gives a dull sound.
watermelon.tip: Spread plastic or straw mulch under the vines to keep fruits clean, hold down weeds and save water.

muskmelon.season: Sow in January to March for summer fruit. In warm regions it can also be sown in November to December.
muskmelon.soil: Well-drained sandy loam, pH 6 to 7.5. Avoid waterlogged and salty fields.
muskmelon.water: Give regular light irrigation during growth and flowering. Reduce water near ripening to improve sweetness and avoid cracking.
muskmelon.fertilizer: Apply farmyard manure and phosphorus at sowing, then split nitrogen and potash during vine growth.
muskmelon.pests: Fruit fly, aphids, powdery mildew and downy mildew are common. Use mulch, fruit fly traps and resistant varieties.
muskmelon.harvest: Ready 80 to 100 days after sowing when the stem slips easily from the fruit and it smells sweet.
muskmelon.tip: Keep fruits off wet soil with straw or mulch to avoid rot and get even colour.

apple.season: Plant dormant grafted saplings in winter (December to February) in cool hills. Trees flower in spring and fruit is picked from July to October.
apple.soil: Deep, well-drained loam, pH 5.5 to 6.5. It needs cold winters and does not tolerate waterlogging.
apple.water: Water young trees in dry spells and during fruit growth. Never let water stand around the trunk.
apple.fertilizer: Apply well-rotted manure in winter and split NPK in spring and after fruit set. Add calcium and boron if fruits show bitter pit or poor set.
apple.pests: Apple scab, woolly aphid, codling moth and root rot are common. Prune for light and air and follow the local spray schedule.
apple.harvest: Pick when seeds turn brown, the fruit separates with a gentle twist and the colour is full for the variety.
apple.tip: Prune in winter to an open shape and thin extra fruitlets so the remaining apples grow larger and the tree bears every year.

orange.season: Plant in July to September with the monsoon, or in February to March. The main harvest is in winter, depending on variety and region.
orange.soil: Well-drained loam or sandy loam, pH 5.5 to 7.5. Waterlogging causes gummosis and root rot.
orange.water: Irrigate every 7 to 15 days in dry months and keep water off the trunk. Dry stress at flowering and fruit set cuts yield.
orange.fertilizer: Give farmyard manure every year and split nitrogen, phosphorus and potash into two or three doses. Add zinc and iron if leaves turn yellow with green veins.
orange.pests: Citrus canker, greening disease, leaf miner and psylla are common. Plant disease-free saplings and remove infected twigs.
orange.harvest: Pick when the fruit has full colour and the right sweetness for the variety, about 8 to 10 months after flowering. Clip fruits with a short stalk.
orange.tip: Keep the graft union at least 30 cm above the ground and the trunk base dry to avoid gummosis.

papaya.season: Transplant seedlings in February to March or September to October, when there is no frost and no heavy rain.
papaya.soil: Well-drained fertile loam, pH 6 to 7. It dies quickly in waterlogged soil, so use raised beds where drainage is poor.
papaya.water: Water every 5 to 7 days in dry months and never let water stand near the stem.
papaya.fertilizer: Feed small doses of nitrogen, phosphorus and potash every two months, along with compost. It responds well to regular feeding.
papaya.pests: Papaya ringspot virus, mealybugs, whitefly and root rot are common. Control insects, remove infected plants early and start with healthy seedlings.
papaya.harvest: Start picking 9 to 11 months after planting when the fruit shows a yellow streak on the skin.
papaya.tip: Plant 2 or 3 seedlings per pit and, once the sex of the plants is clear, keep the female or bisexual plant and remove the extras.

coconut.season: Plant seedlings from June to September with the monsoon. With irrigation, any time except peak summer works.
coconut.soil: Deep, well-drained sandy loam, coastal or laterite soil, pH 5.2 to 8. Avoid long waterlogging.
coconut.water: Needs regular water. In dry months irrigate adult palms every 4 to 7 days by basin or drip.
coconut.fertilizer: Apply organic manure and NPK in split doses every year. Potash is especially important for nut yield.
coconut.pests: Rhinoceros beetle, red palm weevil, eriophyid mite and bud rot occur. Keep the crown clean and use pheromone traps as local experts advise.
coconut.harvest: Nuts are ready 11 to 12 months after the flower opens. Harvest every 45 to 60 days.
coconut.tip: Mulch the basin with coconut husk and leaves to hold moisture and add organic matter.

cotton.season: Kharif: sow in May to June where irrigated, or in June to July with the monsoon in rain-fed areas.
cotton.soil: Deep black soil or well-drained loam, pH 6 to 8. Waterlogging and shallow soil reduce yield.
cotton.water: Irrigate at square formation, flowering and boll development, and avoid water stress at those stages. Drip saves water.
cotton.fertilizer: Apply nitrogen in two or three splits, and phosphorus and potash at sowing. Add farmyard manure before sowing.
cotton.pests: Pink bollworm, whitefly, aphids, jassids and leaf curl virus are common. Scout every week, use pheromone traps and avoid late sowing.
cotton.harvest: Pick fully opened bolls in two or three rounds, from about 150 to 180 days after sowing, on dry days.
cotton.tip: Rotate crops and destroy crop residue after the last picking to cut down pink bollworm.

jute.season: Sow from March to May, when pre-monsoon showers arrive, and harvest in July to September.
jute.soil: Fertile sandy loam to clay loam of river plains, pH 6 to 7.5. Long waterlogging early on harms seedlings.
jute.water: Needs warm, humid weather and good rainfall. Irrigate if rain fails in the first month and keep moisture steady.
jute.fertilizer: Apply farmyard manure at land preparation and split nitrogen along with phosphorus and potash.
jute.pests: Stem weevil, hairy caterpillar, yellow mite and stem rot are common. Thin the plants and weed two or three times.
jute.harvest: Cut plants at 100 to 120 days, when flowers fall and pods form. Ret the bundles in clean, slow water for 10 to 20 days, then strip the fibre.
jute.tip: Thin seedlings to about 5 to 7 cm apart within three weeks of sowing. Crowded plants give weak fibre.

coffee.season: Plant seedlings with the monsoon (June to August) under shade. Arabica is harvested from November to February.
coffee.soil: Fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic loam rich in organic matter, pH 6 to 6.5, on hill slopes with good drainage. Avoid waterlogging.
coffee.water: Needs well-spread rain. Blossom showers or sprinklers in February to March trigger flowering, and mulch holds moisture.
coffee.fertilizer: Apply compost and split NPK before and after the monsoon. Add lime if the soil is too acidic.
coffee.pests: White stem borer, berry borer and leaf rust are the main problems. Keep shade, prune and remove borer-affected stems as local experts advise.
coffee.harvest: Pick ripe red cherries by hand in rounds and process them quickly to keep quality.
coffee.tip: Keep shade trees such as silver oak and prune bushes to an open frame so air and light reach them.
